title: Building the Habit

learn.summary: Technique is worthless without a practice that survives busy weeks; consistency is the single strongest predictor of benefit in program studies. Habit research (Wendy Wood, BJ Fogg) says the levers are a stable cue, a small starting behavior, and low friction, not motivation. Design for your worst day, not your best.

do: Write an if-then plan today ('after I pour my morning coffee, I sit for 5 minutes') and execute it for 7 consecutive days.

children.title: Habit Stacking

learn.summary: Anchor the sit to an existing daily behavior: after brushing teeth, after the school drop-off, after closing the laptop. BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits formula is 'after I [anchor], I will [tiny behavior]', and implementation-intention research (Peter Gollwitzer) shows such if-then plans dramatically raise follow-through. Morning anchors usually win because the day has not yet had a chance to eat your plan.

do: Choose one existing daily anchor and attach a 5-minute sit immediately after it for the next 7 days, tracking hits on paper.

children.title: Minimum Viable Session

learn.summary: Define a floor so small you cannot argue with it: three breaths or one minute counts as a completed day. The point is protecting the identity and the chain, because the real killer is the zero day that becomes a zero week. Most floor days turn into full sessions once you are already sitting.

do: Declare your floor in writing today (e.g. 'three conscious breaths counts') and use it, not zero, on your next impossible day.

children.title: Apps and Timers

learn.summary: Apps like Headspace, Calm, and Insight Timer lower the entry barrier with guided sessions and streaks; RCT evidence for app-based mindfulness shows small-to-moderate short-term benefits. The trap is permanent dependence on guidance, which outsources the noticing. A sensible arc: guided for the first month or two, then a plain timer with occasional guided sessions for new techniques.

do: If you have used guided sessions for over a month, do 2 of your sits this week with a silent timer only.

children.title: Tracking Honestly

learn.summary: Track the behavior (did I sit, for how long), not the vibe (was I peaceful), because vibes are noisy and will convince you that practice is failing during completely normal rough patches. A paper calendar with an X per day is enough. Review monthly, not daily, and judge the trend line, never the single session.

do: Put a calendar where you sit and mark minutes practiced daily for 30 days before drawing any conclusion about how it is going.

reflect: What actually broke your streak last time — the schedule, the room, the expectation? Redesign one of those three.
